name: Chicomuceltec

catalog_citation: Norcliffe, Elizabeth. 2003. The reconstruction of Proto-Huastecan. MA thesis, University of Canterbury (Languages, Cultures and Linguistics), viii+215 pp. hdl:10092/3442, doi:10.26021/4646.
catalog_quote: 2.3 Stress. It is not thought that Proto-Mayan had tone (Kaufman 1986:17), although tonal features have developed in some Mayan languages. Chicomuceltec and Huastec have a stress system, which is not phonemic. In Huastec stress falls on the penultimate syllable when the last syllable is short. It falls on the last syllable if the penultimate syllable is short and the last is long, or if both are long. Chicomuceltec stress, which is marked in Termer's transcriptions, differs from that of Huastec in that it falls consistently on the last syllable. The table below demonstrates the differences in the stress system of the two languages: Chc (T) / H (Vcz): <iník> / ínik 'person'; <pulík> / pú:lek 'big'; <chavál> / čabá:l 'ground'; <k'itá> / k'i:tsá: 'day'

new_statements.relation_note: Language is not in the catalog and has no existing statements, so this is the first explicit stress statement found for Chicomuceltec. It converts our earlier reading's observation (Campbell 1988 forms and Termer 1930 forms carry acute accents almost always on the final syllable, 'transcription practice, not an explicit rule') into an explicit secondary-source rule: fixed final, non-phonemic. It also gives the contrasting Huastec rule (weight-sensitive penult/final), which agrees with the weight-sensitive Huastec placement the huas1242 sources record.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Chicomuceltec stress is non-phonemic (non-contrastive) and falls consistently on the last syllable of the word, in contrast to Huastec, where stress is weight-sensitive (penult when the final syllable is short; final when the final syllable is long, whether or not the penult is long). The Chicomuceltec claim rests on the acute accents in Termer's (1928/1930) transcriptions; the thesis gives four illustrative pairs, all with final accent in Chicomuceltec.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned; the thesis says stress 'falls consistently on the last syllable'. It gives no discussion of how reliable Termer's accent marks are, though elsewhere (pp. 16, 28 ff.) it stresses that vowel length, glottalization and glottal stops are not reliably marked in the Chicomuceltec sources.
new_statements.identity_note: The work covers Chicomuceltec (extinct, Chicomucelo, Chiapas; data from Sapper 1897 and Termer 1928/1930) alongside Huastec, with Huastec forms cited from the Veracruz (Vcz) and Potosi (Pot) dialects. The stress statement for Chicomuceltec is about the language as a whole, based on Termer's transcriptions; the Huastec rule quoted is stated generally, illustrated with Veracruz forms.

sources.citation: Campbell, Lyle. 1988. The Linguistics of Southeast Chiapas, Mexico (Papers of the New World Archaeological Foundation 50). Provo: NWAF/BYU. Ch. 5 'Chicomuceltec', pp. 199-212; References pp. 404-418.
sources.note: Nothing explicit. p.202: 'The total Chicomuceltec corpus is about 500 lexical items.. recorded with no great phonetic accuracy'; defers Huastecan historical phonology to Kaufman 1980. Cited forms from Sapper (S), Termer (T) and the 1970s rememberers carry acute accents, virtually always on the final syllable (p.200: tahbál, kunín / S cuním / T kuním, S ajtíc, tokó / T tokó, to?ól, S osóu / T osóu, S,T vitím, seywé, metát, pičí, S,T chenúk, ač'ám) -- transcription practice only, no rule stated.

sources.citation: Termer, Franz. 1930. Über die Mayasprache von Chicomucelo. Proceedings of the 23rd International Congress of Americanists (New York 1928), pp. 926-936.
sources.note: No statement. Only orthographic remark (p.927): 'In der Orthographie ist die spanische Schreibweise gewählt worden, um eine Vergleichung mit den älteren Aufzeichnungen zu erleichtern.' 284-word vocabulary (with Sapper's list and Stoll's Huaxteca) uses acute accents, not discussed.

sources.note: Nothing on Chicomucelteca stress; the only accent remark in the book (p.288) concerns the Kekchi prayer texts. Word list only.
